detail.title: Denoising Multiple Time Series: Evidence of a Negative Greenium in German Twin Bonds

declarations.funderStatement: C. Bernard gratefully acknowledges funding from the FWO (grant FWOG015320N).

detail.abstract: We begin by introducing a new method for trend extraction in univariate time series, which we call Spline trend filtering. This method combines two established approaches, l1 trend filtering and graduation techniques based on cubic and penalized Splines. The introduced estimator mitigates the ill-conditioning issues associated with the two mentioned methods. We then extend both l1 trend filtering and Spline trend filtering methods to multiple time series regression frameworks, introducing two novel methods that simultaneously denoise multiple interconnected time series while capturing their underlying structural relationships. To manage the computational challenges of large-scale datasets, we implement the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) as an efficient optimization strategy. In our empirical study, we apply the proposed methods to estimate the greenium in the German federal bond market, and we show that investors in Germany are indeed willing to sacrifice part of their profit to support environmental objectives.

title: Spatial Inequalities in U.S. Electric Vehicle Infrastructure
affiliations: and University of Georgia - Warnell School of Forestry and Natural Resources

detail.title: Spatial Inequalities in U.S. Electric Vehicle Infrastructure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no financial or other conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the University of Georgia’s E-Mobility Seed Grant program and the National Science Foundation (grants 2343136 and 2420985).

detail.abstract: Equitable decarbonization depends not only on technology adoption but also on how infrastructure is deployed. Because infrastructure is fixed in space and path dependent, new investments can lock in advantage or exclusion for decades. We examine this dynamic in the case of federal electric vehicle infrastructure, where equity shortfalls are not merely local disparities but structural outcomes of spatial interdependence. Using geospatial analysis and spatial econometric models across 15,566 census tracts in ten southeastern U.S. states, we find that disadvantaged communities are on average 53% farther from federally designated Alternative Fuel Corridors, and that spillovers from neighboring burdens add an additional 10% disadvantage. To test whether inequities are inevitable or policy-contingent, we simulate a counterfactual reallocation aligned with Justice40 mandates. This scenario reduces the average distance gap by 40% and spillover disadvantage by more than 60%. Equity shortfalls in infrastructure transitions thus arise structurally from legacy siting and spatial spillovers, but they are not immutable. Targeted interventions can realign outcomes, showing how network-aware equity frameworks can make the clean energy transition both more just and more effective.

title: Analytical Study of Artificial Intelligence Integration in Indian Banks and Its Implications for the Future of Banking and Financial Services in India
affiliations: NESS Wadia College of Commerce Pune

detail.title: Analytical Study of Artificial Intelligence Integration in Indian Banks and Its Implications for the Future of Banking and Financial Services in India
detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the operational and strategic landscape of the global banking industry, with Indian banks increasingly adopting AIdriven technologies to enhance efficiency, innovation, and customer engagement. This study analytically examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence in Indian banking institutions and evaluates its implications for the future of banking and financial services in India. The research focuses on the adoption patterns of AI technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and robotic process automation across both public and private sector banks. Using secondary data from reports published by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), NITI Aayog, and major financial institutions, the study explores how AI contributes to improving operational efficiency, risk management, fraud detection, and personalized service delivery. The paper also investigates the challenges associated with AI implementation, including data privacy concerns, skill gaps, regulatory compliance, and ethical considerations. The findings indicate that while AI integration has significantly improved service quality and decision-making processes, its long-term sustainability depends on robust digital infrastructure, regulatory frameworks, and workforce upskilling. The study concludes that Artificial Intelligence will play a pivotal role in shaping the future of the Indian banking sector by promoting financial inclusion, enhancing competitiveness, and fostering a more resilient and customer-centric banking ecosystem.

detail.title: The Language of a Place

detail.abstract:
Chapter Excerpt:
...In recent years, I have conducted formal, one-on-one interviews on a folding chair next to a cow pasture and worn t-shirts and shorts for semi-structured focus groups. I mention these things not as indicators of “rural” but because I think this is what happens when people are after the same things together for a relatively long time. In other words, when people are invested in your research and want to get the story right—i.e., as nuanced and multidimensional as possible—there is very little pretense. After seven years, people know that I have the training, resources, and networks to amplify their expertise and the work they’re doing. It doesn’t matter that the air conditioner at the Tribal housing authority is broken and we’re all in shorts; it matters that we all showed up. What is potentially “rural” about it, then, is me: I desperately don’t want to recreate the experience Kathy Cramer recounted, of the distanced, “liberal elite,” researcher who could’ve just asked.  

But there is something more, which is the matter of love. I have invited collaborating judges to co-author articles and participate in academic conferences, and they have invited me to concerts and pow wows. My daughters call one Tribal court judge “auntie,” and this winter a district court judge invited me to her wedding. When I went through my divorce, two separate judges called me almost monthly to check in. Through my research on rural access to justice, I, and my family, have become deeply enmeshed in the lives of others.

title: Physical Disaster Shocks and Public Debt: A Dynamic Model of Fiscal Federalism
affiliations: Southwest Jiaotong University - School of Economics & Management

detail.title: Physical Disaster Shocks and Public Debt: A Dynamic Model of Fiscal Federalism
detail.abstract: This study develops a dynamic general equilibrium model to analyze how physical disasters amplify public debt in decentralized fiscal systems. Using a purely analytical model, we compare Markov (no commitment) and Ramsey (full commitment) equilibria. We find that disaster severity increases debt at both government levels. Crucially, the absence of commitment induces myopic spending and fiscal instability, while commitment enables efficient risk-sharing and sustainable debt trajectories through rules-based transfer systems. Our main contribution is to demonstrate analytically how commitment mechanisms in intergovernmental transfers can mitigate disaster-induced debt accumulation, providing a theoretical foundation for fiscal rules in decentralized systems.

title: Determinants of Short-Term Debt in Private Firms: A Return to Fundamentals
affiliations: Free University of Bolzano - Faculty of Economics and Management, Free University of Bozen-Bolzano and Free University of Bozen-Bolzano

detail.title: Determinants of Short-Term Debt in Private Firms: A Return to Fundamentals
detail.abstract: We construct a capital structure index with three unique features. First, the index links revenue growth to the capital structure through firm fundamentals. Second, the index coefficient predicts the capital structure of individual firms and, through aggregation, industries, distinguishing those that experience sustainable growth from those requiring external funding to grow. Third, the index explains both inter-and intra-industry heterogeneity in capital structure. In our empirical analysis, we show that the proposed index explains and predicts the short-term financial position for individual firms and industries. We validate the index using a large dataset of European private firms and find stronger support for fundamentals as the primary determinant of private firms' capital structures. The results remain robust across various model specifications and leverage measures. We contribute to the literature by offering a single index that distinguishes between firms and industries capable of selfreliant growth and those requiring short-term financing.

title: Machine Governance: An Institutional Theory of Human-AI Delegation
affiliations: RMIT University

detail.title: Machine Governance: An Institutional Theory of Human-AI Delegation
detail.abstract: Delegation is the organising principle of economic life. As decision-making authority passes from humans to artificial systems, the institutional logic of delegation is transformed. Traditional governance rests on incentives, monitoring, and trust; these presume intention and opportunism. Machines exhibit neither. Their failures arise not from moral hazard but from divergence between representation and reality. The paper reformulates principal-agent theory for human-AI relations by extending the institutional analysis of Coase, Williamson, North, and Buchanan into the domain of artificial agency. It identifies ontological hazard as the characteristic risk of machine delegation and develops constraint compatibility as the corresponding condition for governance. Enforcement migrates from law to architecture; authority relocates from discretion to design. The economy of governance becomes one of verification rather than motivation, bounded by the costs of proving that systems function as intended. To remain legitimate, institutions must embed corrigibility: the capacity to audit, interpret, and revise machine operations without forfeiting efficiency. The constitutional task of the twenty-first century is therefore to design architectures of decision that preserve human accountability while containing autonomous execution.

title: Measuring Expectations in Real Estate Markets from Long-Term Lease Contracts

detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel methodology to extract rent growth expectations from commercial leases based on an asset pricing framework. Using over 20 years of data for office, industrial, and retail leases across major U.S. markets, we estimate the spot rent index (SRI), growth expectations, and risk premiums for each market. The SRIs capture economic cycles in a timely manner. Rent growth expectations vary significantly by property type, market, lease term, and time period, while risk premiums vary substantially across markets. This study provides new measures of firms' inflation expectations for commercial real estate, a significant component of national wealth.

title: Distance to the Border and Cross-Border Fuel Shopping: Evidence from Albania and Montenegro
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Norwegian University of Life Sciences and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Distance to the Border and Cross-Border Fuel Shopping: Evidence from Albania and Montenegro
detail.abstract: This study examines how consumers respond to price differentials by analyzing cross-border fuel purchasing between Albania and Montenegro. Using station-level sales data from 2020–2024, we find clear evidence of substitution: when Montenegrin prices fall relative to Albanian prices, fuel sales at nearby Albanian stations decline, with the strongest effects within 20 kilometers of the border. During Covid-19 border closures, this effect disappears, confirming the role of cross-border shopping. The response is more pronounced for diesel than for gasoline, potentially reflecting the fact that trucks, whose route often crosses this border, are flexible in their choice of where to buy fuel.

title: Fiscal Decentralisation and Governance in Hargaisa Local Government, Somaliland
affiliations: , Kampala International University and Kampala International University

detail.title: Fiscal Decentralisation and Governance in Hargaisa Local Government, Somaliland
detail.abstract: Background: Fiscal decentralisation is pivotal for governance in fragile states like Somaliland. Hargeisa Local Government emphasises community participation but faces funding shortages, weak institutions, and the exclusion of marginalised groups, hindering effective service delivery. Objective: To critically analyse the relationship between fiscal decentralisation and governance in Hargaisa Local Government, Somaliland. Method: A mixed-methods correlational survey was employed, collecting data from 269 officials across nine districts. Quantitative data were collected using Likert-scale questionnaires, which were analysed via SPSS (descriptive/inferential statistics), supplemented by structured qualitative interviews that were subjected to thematic analysis. Result: Fiscal decentralisation strongly correlated with improved governance (β = 0.623, *p* < 0.001), enhancing accountability, transparency, and e-governance. However, constraints included limited taxation authority (mean = 2.53), dependence on external grants (mean = 2.71), and weak community participation (mean = 2.49). Demographic barriers were evident, including gender disparities (60.2% male workforce) and mid-level bureaucratic dominance (40.1%). Conclusion: Fiscal decentralisation significantly boosts governance quality but requires complementary reforms to address institutional weaknesses and structural inequities. Unique Contribution: This study validates the Soufflé Theory in a fragile state context, demonstrating that balanced political, administrative, and fiscal decentralisation can strengthen local governance without fragmenting national cohesion. It identifies structural barriers (e.g., gender gaps, revenue dependency) specific to post-conflict settings. Key Recommendation: Strengthen local revenue systems via expanded taxation authority; institutionalise participatory budgeting and gender-inclusive policies; and scale e-governance tools to enhance transparency. Central governments should provide oversight while empowering local fiscal autonomy.

title: The Economics of Belief: Personality, Narrative, and the Architecture of Power in Contemporary India

detail.title: The Economics of Belief: Personality, Narrative, and the Architecture of Power in Contemporary India
detail.abstract: This article argues that contemporary Indian politics is fundamentally shaped by narrative power, and that the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) functions less as an administrative centre than as the command hub of the nation’s “narrative economy.” Drawing on Robert Shiller’s theory of narrative economics, it contends that political legitimacy, public trust, and economic confidence in India are increasingly driven by stories that resonate, repeat, and spread like epidemics. Examining India’s post-independence leadership: from Nehru’s modernist vision and Indira Gandhi’s centralised authority to Vajpayee’s poetic nationalism and Modi’s digitally-enabled populism; the paper shows how Prime Ministers have crafted and institutionalised narratives that shape national identity and policy reception. In the Modi era especially, the PMO has become a highly coordinated machinery of narrative production, integrating communication strategy, bureaucracy, and digital platforms to maintain story discipline and sustain a personality-driven political economy. While dominant narratives can unify and mobilise the nation, they also carry risks: over-personalisation of leadership, erosion of institutional autonomy, and vulnerability to sudden narrative breakdown when belief falters. Ultimately, the paper argues that narrative power in India remains contested, even when highly centralised, and that understanding the PMO as a “story factory” is essential to explaining both contemporary governance and the politics of legitimacy in the world’s largest democracy.

title: Assessing Co-optimisation: Coordination Effects vs. Cross-Zonal Capacity Allocation in Markets for Balancing Capacity and Scheduled Energy
affiliations: RWTH Aachen University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, RWTH Aachen University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Assessing Co-optimisation: Coordination Effects vs. Cross-Zonal Capacity Allocation in Markets for Balancing Capacity and Scheduled Energy
detail.abstract: To ensure efficiency of market-based procurement of balancing services, the EU Guideline on Electricity Balancing aims at harmonising and integrating balancing service markets across Europe, including exchange of balancing capacity. A key challenge for the exchange of balancing capacity is that balancing capacity markets clear before day-ahead markets for scheduled energy, requiring prior allocation of cross-zonal transmission capacity. The EU Guideline on Electricity Balancing outlines several approaches for handling cross-zonal capacity in the context of balancing capacity exchange, including the co-optimised allocation process. This process allocates cross-zonal capacity based on actual bids from both markets, requiring simultaneous clearing and introducing significant implementation complexity. Co-optimisation has two main effects: in theory, it enables improved coordination of bids across markets and achieves optimal cross-zonal capacity allocation at day-ahead time. A recent study highlighted substantial welfare gains from co-optimisation but primarily captured coordination effects between generation units, overlooking existing portfolio-based coordination by market participants. To isolate the specific impact of balancing capacity exchange, this paper develops a methodology to compare cases without such exchange, assuming both full and no coordination of units, to a case with exchange and co-optimised allocation. The results indicate that welfare gains from coordination between units exceed those from co-optimisation of markets.

title: From Time-Series Momentum to Size-Factor Comovement: Bitcoin's Continuing Evolution as a Financial Asset
affiliations: Temple University, Fox School of Business and

detail.title: From Time-Series Momentum to Size-Factor Comovement: Bitcoin's Continuing Evolution as a Financial Asset
detail.abstract: We study the evolution of Bitcoin (BTC) as a financial asset using weekly return data from 2011 to 2024. In the early years, BTC returns were predictable based on past returns (time-series momentum) and investor attention. In recent years, however, these predictors have lost explanatory power, consistent with increasing market efficiency and the absence of arbitrage opportunities. While BTC has long comoved with broad macro-financial indicators such as the VIX and the two-year Treasury yield, its comovement with traditional equity factors has emerged only more recently. Since 2019, BTC returns have become significantly correlated with the Fama-French size factor, indicating that Bitcoin now behaves, in part, like a small-cap stock. Together, these findings document Bitcoin's transition from an anarcho-libertarian speculative investment to a mainstream financial asset increasingly integrated with traditional markets.

title: The Power of Words: Central Bank Green Communication and Performance of Energy Sectors
affiliations: Autonomous University of Barcelona and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Power of Words: Central Bank Green Communication and Performance of Energy Sectors
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the effect of climate- and energy-related (green) communication by the European Central Bank (ECB) on the performance of renewable and fossil-based energy sectors. Using a sentence-embedding natural language processing method, we identify 247 ECB speeches from 2015 to 2024 that explicitly reference both climate and energy themes, categorize them, and compute a green score for each. The analysis reveals prominent topics of climate and financial risk, and monetary policy and economic conditions, along with consistently positive and trust-related emotional cues. We then use high-frequency identification to estimate the effect of ECB green speeches on the return differential between the green and the brown energy sectors. The results show that such ECB communication positively and significantly affects sectoral relative returns, highlighting the communicative role of the ECB in influencing the relative performance of green and brown energy sectors. The results remain robust across a series of sensitivity analyses. The effect does not change significantly with respect to the outbreak of the Russian--Ukrainian war or the ECB communication topics.

title: Passing as White: Racial Identity and Old-Age Longevity
affiliations: Texas Tech University and University of Wisconsin-Madison - Robert M. La Follette School of Public Affairs

detail.title: Passing as White: Racial Identity and Old-Age Longevity
detail.abstract: In the presence of segregation and discrimination during the late 19th and early 20th century, many African American men changed their racial identity and “passed” for white. Previous studies have suggested that this activity was associated with increases in income and socioeconomic status despite the costs associated with cutting ties with their black communities. This study adds to this literature by evaluating the long-run effects of passing on old-age longevity. We construct longitudinal data of black families in historical censuses (1880-1940) linked to their male children’s Social Security Administration death records (1975-2005). We use family fixed effects to demonstrate that individuals passing as white live approximately 9.4 months longer, on average, than their non-passing siblings. Additional analyses suggest substantial improvements in education and occupational standing scores as well as differential parental investments as potential pathways.

title: Strengthening Rapid Education Response in Acute Emergencies Democratic Republic of the Congo Country Report
affiliations: University of Antwerp - Institute of Development Policy

detail.title: Strengthening Rapid Education Response in Acute Emergencies Democratic Republic of the Congo Country Report
detail.abstract: With generous contribution from, and in partnership with the European Commission's Directorate-General for Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations (DG ECHO), the Global Education Cluster together with UNICEF, Save the Children, UNESCO International Institute for Educational Planning (IIEP), REACH, NORCAP, and Translators without Borders to address barriers preventing girls and boys living in situations of humanitarian crisis from realizing their right to receive quality education. Specifically, the partners developed evidence, tools, and a training to strengthen rapid education responses, including through Rapid Response Mechanisms, to ensure children's life-saving and life sustaining education needs are addressed in the first phase of humanitarian response.

title: The Heterogeneous Effects of Large and Small Minimum Wage Changes on Hours Worked: Evidence Using a Partially Pre-Committed Analysis Plan
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) and American Enterprise Institute

detail.title: The Heterogeneous Effects of Large and Small Minimum Wage Changes on Hours Worked: Evidence Using a Partially Pre-Committed Analysis Plan
detail.abstract: We use a partially pre-committed estimation strategy to study the effects of minimum wage increases on hours worked. We estimate that large minimum wage increases reduced usual hours worked per week among individuals with low levels of experience and education by just under one hour per week during the decade prior to the Covid-19 pandemic, while the effects of smaller minimum wage increases are economically and statistically indistinguishable from zero. Our estimates are directly comparable with, and ultimately similar to, estimates of extensive-margin employment elasticities in response to the same set of minimum wage increases.

title: The force of the main-course in Norwegian wage formation, 1900-2024
affiliations: University of Oslo - Department of Economics, Statistics Norway and Statistics Norway

detail.title: The force of the main-course in Norwegian wage formation, 1900-2024
detail.abstract: Using time series from a new database with historical time series for Norway, we investigate the strength—or rather, the force—of the main-course variable, defined by the manufacturing sector, in explaining the yearly wage. Using impulse and step indicator saturation, we obtain robust coefficient estimates and test their stability in the presence of structural breaks. We find a high degree of parameter constancy in the relationship between wages and the main-course variable. Our findings support interpreting the maincourse as a super-exogenous variable in the wage equation. This implies that the maincourse has been a persistent and powerful driver of national wage levels for over 120 years, extending well beyond the boundaries of manufacturing. The results align with the historical development of labour market regulation: the retained break indicators mainly correspond to years in the 1920s and 1930s, marked by large-scale industrial disputes but also the beginning of more coordinated collective bargaining. The model also aligns well with the institutional reality of the 2020s. The manufacturing sector’s collective agreement continues to serve as the “front-runner” in Norway’s system of pattern wage bargaining.

title: Adam Smith and Sympathetic Cosmopolitanism
affiliations: Trinity University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Adam Smith and Sympathetic Cosmopolitanism
detail.abstract:
Is cosmopolitanism something to explain or is it the lack of cosmopolitanism that needs explaining? Is cosmopolitanism natural or something we need to try to achieve? Is cosmopolitanism an end result or a starting point? The answer depends on the anthropological assumptions one makes. If human beings are assumed to be isolated individuals, then cosmopolitanism is something to explain, something to be taught, a possible end result. But if human beings are assumed to be intrinsically and naturally social, then cosmopolitanism may be a starting point and what needs to be explained is its absence.

I suggest that for Adam Smith humans are intrinsically social and thus his starting point is cosmopolitanism. Given human natural sociability, part of Smith’s task is to explain the absence of cosmopolitanism, which he attributes to either dire living conditions or the ability of some special interest groups to affect public opinion to their benefits.

title: Closed-Form Analysis of Congested Networks: Isolating the Impact of Topology on Market Outcomes
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Closed-Form Analysis of Congested Networks: Isolating the Impact of Topology on Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: This paper maps sets out to answer the question how far closed-form reasoning can take us before resorting to numerical simulations, in studying congested zonal power markets. Operational realism was traded for tractability in order to isolate what network structure alone can explain about market fragility, burden sharing, and economic efficiency. Managing congestion and price volatility is central to electricity market design, yet topology's role is often obscured by complex simulations. We developed a tractable model using algebraic graph theory to derive equilibrium prices for all congestion regimes in canonical three-zone line and loop topologies. We introduced capacity-space metrics—-- Fragility Area (FA), Integrated Price Volume (IPV), and Integrated Welfare Volume (IWV) --—that quantify price volatility prevalence, average burden distribution, and total economic surplus across transmission capacity configurations. Three results emerge. First, radial networks create volatility hubs when price-inelastic zones lie in transit, exhibiting broad fragility regions and unequal burden sharing. Second, introducing a single redundant link produces a structural regime shift: FA curves display cliff-like collapses, IPV shares converge toward equal distribution, and total welfare increases 11--15\%, with 70\% of gains realized at modest redundant capacity. Third, additional capacity yields diminishing returns, indicating that connectivity and redundancy--— not connection capacity alone --—drive market resilience. Welfare gains are broadly shared but concentrate where economic activity is greatest, with vulnerable inelastic zones benefiting disproportionately.These closed-form solutions and diagnostics provide benchmarks that agent-based or optimization studies can validate and extend; our goal is to establish theory that simulations should reproduce, not to replace them.

title: Adam Smith and the Division of Labor
affiliations: Trinity University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Adam Smith and the Division of Labor
detail.abstract: For Adam Smith, people need to be free to receive the fruits of their labor both because it is their right and also because it will give incentives to produce more and innovate more. Increased production and innovation will generate the prosperity that brings people out of absolute poverty. They create the means to support a growing population, and a cheerful society.

title: Built to Move: We Need Everyday Activity More Than Gym Sessions
affiliations: Aalborg University

detail.title: Built to Move: We Need Everyday Activity More Than Gym Sessions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This essay argues that modern health and longevity depend more on incorporating frequent, natural movement into everyday life than on occasional gym workouts. Drawing on evolutionary biology, anthropology and public health research, it explores how our ancestors' physical activity patterns, characterised by constant motion and purposeful rest, contrast with today's sedentary routines. Through an examination of hunter-gatherer societies, the concept of Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis (NEAT) and behaviours observed in the global 'Blue Zones', the essay demonstrates that simple actions such as walking, climbing stairs, squatting and social movement can have a significant impact on health. It suggests practical strategies for restoring a lifestyle that is better suited to our evolutionary design.

detail.abstract: This article compares two systems of labour market governance: regulation by means of employment standards, and norms that are established in collective bargaining. A comparative framework draws nine criteria, spanning procedural and substantive dimensions, and emphasises the degree of integration between the systems, or "coupling." The study uses Israel's response to the COVID-19 crisis as a case study, drawing on a unique dataset of all regulatory provisions and collective agreements concluded from March 2020 to December 2021, supplemented by interviews with key actors. In the public sector, strong coupling was achieved through coordinated regulatory and bargaining processes, resulting in more adaptive, legitimate, and effective governance. In contrast, the private sector exhibited loose coupling, marked by fragmented bargaining and limited regulatory engagement, which undermined coordinated responses to labour market disruptions. The study concludes that tight coupling enhances governance outcomes, especially in times of crisis. It argues for greater attention to the substance of collective agreements and the interaction between governance systems. While the findings are context-specific, the proposed analytical framework offers broader applicability for comparative labour law and policy.

title: Investment Effects of a Quasi-Robot Tax: Evidence from South Korea
affiliations: University of Mannheim - Accounting and Taxation, Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt, Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich - Department of Economics, Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt and Catholic University of Eichstaett-Ingolstadt

detail.title: Investment Effects of a Quasi-Robot Tax: Evidence from South Korea
detail.abstract: We study a 2018 reform in South Korea that reduced tax credits for automation investments. This reform increased the tax cost of investing in robots and thus resembles a robot tax. Exploiting this natural experiment with industry-level data on robot installations and firm-level data from Orbis, we document a sharp decline in automation investments after the reform in industries with a large share of affected firms. At the firm level, we find that affected firms increased employment, consistent with the notion that robots replaced workers. The effects are heterogeneous: financially constrained firms cut investment overall, while unconstrained firms substituted away from robots, hired more workers, and reallocated resources toward more productive uses. For the latter group, we find improvements in various measures of investment quality, suggesting that the tax credit induced inefficient overinvestment in automation. Our evidence informs ongoing debates on robot taxation and the efficiency of tax incentives.

title: The Financial Cost of Biodiversity Loss for SMEs
affiliations: ICMA Centre, Henley Business School, University of Reading, ICMA Centre - Henley Business School, University of Reading, University of Reading - ICMA Centre, Natural History Museum and Natural History Museum

detail.title: The Financial Cost of Biodiversity Loss for SMEs
detail.abstract: In this study, we investigate the impact of biodiversity loss on the performance of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the United Kingdom and Ireland. Leveraging firms' financial information and the Biodiversity Intactness Index — a geospatial dataset at a 10 and 1 km 2 developed by the Natural History Museum — we geo-locate SMEs, quantify biodiversity loss where firms operate, and assess their exposure to biodiversity-related risks over time. Our findings indicate that a one standard-deviation decline in local biodiversity leads to a statistically significant reduction in firm operating profit by 0.74 percentage points. This effect appears to operate primarily through higher operating costs and is economically meaningful as it corresponds to about 36% of the sample's average operating profit to total assets ratio. Moreover, micro firms and SMEs located in more ecologically degraded areas are found to be more exposed to biodiversity-related risks. This reinforces our main findings, showing that biodiversity exposure is not uniform across firms but is amplified by both local ecological conditions and firm scale. The results remain robust across alternative econometric specifications and after controlling for climate risk factors.

title: Innovation, Knowledge and Institutional Development in Colombia Institutional Development

detail.title: Innovation, Knowledge and Institutional Development in Colombia Institutional Development
detail.abstract: This article analyzes Title I of the 1991 Political Constitution of Colombia from the analytical framework of economic development proposed by Nobel laureates Joel Mokyr , Philippe Aghion, and Peter Howitt. It examines whether the fundamental principles of the constitutional text facilitate an institutional model oriented toward investment in knowledge, a culture of innovation, and regulated competition. Through a hermeneutic and comparative approach, it argues that the Constitution incorporates potential elements for development based on creative destruction, provided that social safety nets exist to balance technological change and territorial equity.

title: Management Of Guaranteed Debt: Shortcomings And Ways For Improvement

detail.title: Management Of Guaranteed Debt: Shortcomings And Ways For Improvement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Economic journal of Lesya Ukrainka Volyn National University, volume 3, issue 43, 2025[10.29038/2786-4618-2025-03-88-95]

detail.abstract:
State-guaranteed debt arises from borrowings by economic entities for the implementation of infrastructure projects under state guarantees, which offers advantages provided there is effective control and minimal corruption risks. However, the imperfection of Ukraine's practice in managing guaranteed debt leads to an increase in residents' indebtedness, which transforms into guaranteed debt, while a significant portion of projects remains unimplemented, highlighting the need for improving the monitoring system. 

State-guaranteed debt constitutes a contingent liability that arises due to the inability of residents to fulfill debt obligations obtained under state guarantees. The absence of a clear methodology for assessing the creditworthiness of economic entities, a specialized management body, and transparent project selection procedures increases corruption risks and threatens debt security. International experience confirms that ineffective management of guaranteed debt leads to a crowding-out effect on investments, hindering economic development. Inadequate control over the use of loans exacerbates the financial burden on the state budget. This necessitates a revision of approaches to providing guarantees to ensure their effectiveness. 

The shortcomings in the management of guaranteed debt in Ukraine, particularly the lack of transparency and creditworthiness assessment, create fiscal risks. There is a need to improve legislation, project selection procedures, and establish a specialized body to enhance efficiency and strengthen debt security. Further research should focus on developing clear criteria for assessing borrowers' solvency and creating a specialized body for managing guaranteed debt to reduce corruption risks and increase the effectiveness of state guarantees.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the long-horizon predictive variance of an international bond strategy where a U.S. investor holds unhedged positions in constant-maturity long-term foreign bonds funded at domestic short-term interest rates. Using over two centuries of data from major economies, the study finds that predictive variance grows with the investment horizon, driven primarily by uncertainties in interest rate differentials and exchange rate returns, which outweigh mean reversion effects. The analysis, incorporating both observable and unobservable predictors, highlights that unobservable predictors linked to shifts in monetary and exchange rate regimes are the dominant source of long-term risk, offering fresh insights into international bond investment strategies.

detail.title: Liquidity and Trading Dynamics in the Off-the-Run U.S. Treasury Market

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of New York Staff Report No. 1170
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this article, we study trading activity and liquidity of off-the-run U.S. Treasury securities. Off-the-run Treasuries are seasoned securities, account for about 98 percent of all Treasuries outstanding, and played a central role in the pandemic-fueled dash-for-cash in March 2020. Understanding these securities better can improve thinking around how market resilience might be improved. We document and discuss the evolution of trading activity and liquidity for these securities and how these attributes differ from on-therun securities. We also consider several potential market structure changes that could improve the liquidity of off-the-run Treasuries, including debt buybacks, expanded central clearing, and increased data transparency.

title: Curvature and Contingencies: Pricing Lease Term Risk in Commercial Real Estate
affiliations: University of Central Florida, Auburn University - Department of Finance, Florida State University and University of South Florida

detail.title: Curvature and Contingencies: Pricing Lease Term Risk in Commercial Real Estate
detail.abstract: Lease duration presents landlords with a fundamental choice: secure near-term cash flows or preserve flexibility for uncertain future states. We document that commercial property markets price this trade-off with considerable sophistication. Analyzing 8,293 U.S. single-tenant transactions (2000-2019), we find capitalization rates compress steeply with term initially but flatten substantially beyond 20 years-a convexity explained by competing insurance (against near-term rollover) and encumbrance (from long-horizon uncertainty) effects. We develop an option-theoretic framework that predicts this curvature and its systematic variation. Testing these predictions, we find the curve's shape varies with tenant reliability, property characteristics, market tightness, and climate exposure. These findings extend real-options leasing models, quantify heterogeneity absent in prior aggregate studies, and offer practical insights for lease structuring and portfolio management amid multidimensional trade-offs between certainty and flexibility.

detail.abstract: Whether the marginal utility of consumption differs by health status is a key input to many economic models. However, evidence on the sign and magnitude of state dependence between consumption and health remains mixed. Using detailed panel data from Singapore that measures consumption and health each month, we find that health and consumption are complements. The marginal utility of consumption increases by 3.5% for a one-standard deviation increase in an index of health based on chronic conditions. Simulations illustrate our estimates of state dependence have quantitatively important implications for optimal retirement saving.

title: Hidden Reservoirs: The Role of Soils and Forests during Droughts
affiliations: World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: Hidden Reservoirs: The Role of Soils and Forests during Droughts
detail.abstract: Droughts are widely recognized for their adverse effects on economies, especially on agriculture. With approximately 75% of global food production occurring under rainfed conditions understanding the role of soil moisture is critical. Yet its influence on the economic impacts of drought remains poorly understood. Using global gridded data spanning 25 years, we find that locations with higher pre-shock root-zone soil moisture are associated with smaller drought-year growth losses. We also study a plausible determinant of elevated soil moisture-upstream forest cover-and find that grid cells with greater upstream forest cover correlate with higher soil moisture storage and exhibit losses about half as large as in low-forest settings. Taken together, the evidence highlights the potential value of considering soil moisture and its forest-based drivers alongside conventional "blue" water management, and climate adaptation strategies.

title: Optimizing Retirement Financial Strategies: Integrating Annuities, Defined Contribution Plans, and Long-Term Care Costs
affiliations: Goethe University Frankfurt - Finance Department, Goethe University Frankfurt - Finance Department ,  and Goethe University Frankfurt - Department of Finance

detail.title: Optimizing Retirement Financial Strategies: Integrating Annuities, Defined Contribution Plans, and Long-Term Care Costs

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Nursing home costs in the United States now exceed $100,000 per year, and government assistance programs such as Medicaid help out only when retirees are largely destitute. Moreover, health shocks driving the need for such care can arise suddenly in old age, are frequently permanent in nature, and can be associated with declining mental and physical abilities. These facts raise the important question of how households can best prepare to finance this final phase of life. Building on past research, we determine how retirees should manage payouts from defined contribution plans to balance trade-offs between consumption and health care cost shocks, using both retirement plan assets and annuitization. Our analysis explicitly integrates the role of taxes, required minimum distributions, bequest motives, and the possibility of retiree insolvency. We conclude that payout annuities, especially deferred and variable annuities, can be quite valuable for retirees, even when they face health shocks in later life.

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We examine what is widely considered to be one of the strongest channels of monetary policy transmission into household spending – the effect of changes in mortgage payments when mortgage rates are linked to the short-term policy rate. Using bank transactions data from Australia, we analyze a cumulative 425 basis point increase in the central bank policy rate, which caused mortgage repayments for homeowners with adjustable-rate mortgages to increase by $13,800. We find little change in the spending of adjustable-rate mortgagors relative to fixed rate mortgagors. This is because adjustable-rate mortgages come with redraw facilities that make mortgages liquid, and households had large excess buffers due to pandemic-era transfer programs and restrictions on spending. Our findings demonstrate that the direct effects of a monetary policy tightening on household spending need not be large.

title: The Implications of Sorting for Immigrant Wage Assimilation and Changing Cohort Quality in Canada
affiliations: Queen's University (Canada), Faculty of Arts & Science, Department of Economics, Students and

detail.title: The Implications of Sorting for Immigrant Wage Assimilation and Changing Cohort Quality in Canada

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Immigrant integration is a central issue in policy debates, with wage assimilation serving as a key indicator of immigrants’ economic success. Using matched employer–employee data from Canada, we study how access to higher-paying firms affects the economic assimilation of immigrants. Immigrants are disproportionately concentrated in lower-paying firms, accounting for much of the observed inequality. Nearly half of this sorting occurs across industries, and both firm- and industry-level wage gaps stagnate after eight years, suggesting that further assimilation reflects human capital accumulation rather than improved firm access. Importantly, these disparities persist after controlling for estimates of worker skill, indicating barriers to high-paying firms rather than differences in human capital. The analysis further shows that Canada’s post-2015 immigration policy reforms significantly improved immigrant outcomes: the initial wage gap narrowed by 25–35%, with roughly half of the improvement attributable to better allocation into higher-paying firms. Taken together, the findings highlight the critical role of firm sorting and its interaction with immigration policy in shaping the economic integration of immigrants.

title: Is Video Watching Bad for Kids? The Effect of Video Watching on Children's Skills
affiliations: University of Georgia, University of Georgia, Tennessee Technological University and University of Georgia

detail.title: Is Video Watching Bad for Kids? The Effect of Video Watching on Children's Skills

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper documents video consumption among school-aged children in the U.S. and explores its impact on human capital development. Video watching is common across all segments of society, yet surprisingly little is known about its developmental consequences. With a bunching identification strategy, we find that an additional hour of daily video consumption has a negative impact on children’s noncognitive skills, with harmful effects on both internalizing behaviors (e.g., depression) and externalizing behaviors (e.g., social difficulties). We find a positive effect on math skills, though the effect on an aggregate measure of cognitive skills is smaller and not statistically significant. These findings are robust and largely stable across most demographics and different ways of measuring skills and video watching. We find evidence that for Hispanic children, video watching has positive effects on both cognitive and noncognitive skills—potentially reflecting its role in supporting cultural assimilation. Interestingly, the marginal effects of video watching remain relatively stable regardless of how much time children spend on the activity, with similar incremental impacts observed among those who watch very little and those who watch for many hours.

title: Does Public Health Insurance Cause Crowding Into Public Facilities and Informality? The Case of Seguro Popular
affiliations: Yale University, University of California, Berkeley and El Colegio de Mexico

detail.title: Does Public Health Insurance Cause Crowding Into Public Facilities and Informality? The Case of Seguro Popular

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Many low and middle-income countries are working to expand health insurance to previously uncovered people by creating health insurance programs intended for low-income people who would otherwise lack insurance coverage. Two concerns have been raised about these programs. First, people may be “crowded out” of private facilities and into public ones, increasing public expense and possibly degrading care through crowding. Second, public insurance could encourage informality by reducing the gap in compensation between formal sector and informal sector workers. We examine these questions in the context of Mexico’s Seguro Popular (SP) using longitudinal administrative data on childbirth. We focus on women with more than one observed birth and ask how SP affects the choice of provider for those whose first observed birth was in a public hospital, a private hospital, or a separate system of hospitals serving formal sector workers. We also look at how SP affects the utilization of care and newborn health. Because SP enrollment is endogenous, we instrument it using the rollout of a second program, SMSXXI, that provided health care for young children and enrolled other family members in SP. We find that the expansion of SMSXXI increased SP coverage of pregnant women. This in turn led to a higher probability of delivering in a public hospital, especially among those who had previously delivered in a private hospital. We find little impact of SP enrollment on the utilization of care or newborn health, with the notable exception that women who previously delivered in a private hospital were more likely to start prenatal care in the first trimester when they switched to SP, indicating a greater willingness to seek preventive care when it is free.

detail.abstract: The channels of routine are worn deep into the fabric of the equilibrium that characterizes the existing order. Gradually, economic life settles into a repetitive pattern where risk must be negotiated but uncertainty has disappeared. The order benefits some more than others, but most people, even those who are not faring well, will develop an attachment to it, afraid of what change could mean for them. Others, dissatisfied with the status quo they have been trapped in by the destiny of time and place, await the arrival of change, any change. The entrepreneur is the agent of change. Not from within the equilibrium, but from without it. He upsets the existing order, destroying the old, and creating the new. The vested interests of the old order and those who depend upon them along with those who fear any change to the status quo will resist the entrepreneur’s innovation. In this, they might be successful. Or they may fail. In that territory where finance intersects with international affairs, the power structures that depended on the old order, on routine finance, are upended along with the finance industry itself.

title: Path Dependence in the Labor Market: The Long-run Effects of Early Career Occupational Experience
affiliations: Brown University, ISO New England, , Tufts University, U.S. Department of the Treasury, Office of Tax Analysis (OTA) and United States Military Academy, West Point

detail.title: Path Dependence in the Labor Market: The Long-run Effects of Early Career Occupational Experience

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study the causal effect of different early career occupational experiences on labor market outcomes. To do so, we pair over two decades of administrative tax data with internal personnel records from one of the largest employers of young adults in the United States: the US Army. Enlistees work in a diverse and varied set of occupations, including non-combat roles like mechanics, legal services, financial specialists, cooks, dental hygienists, police officers, and network/computer specialists. Occupational eligibility is determined by test score cutoffs which we leverage in a series of 35 regression discontinuity designs. We find that a typical early career occupational experience generates a substantial amount of path dependence, with point estimates that suggest a 19p.p. increase in the likelihood of being observed in an identical or closely related occupation as much as 20 years later. The corresponding impact of different occupations on earnings are highly heterogeneous, yet predictable: long-run changes in the average earnings of the occupations applicants are pushed into, and pulled out-of, can explain over 60% of the causal variation across cutoffs, with point estimates that suggest improvements in occupational earnings premia translate dollar-for-dollar into economic success. Taken together, our results highlight the importance of early career occupational experience as a key channel for promoting long-run well-being among young adults who are not college bound.

detail.title: Mortgage Lending in Sundown Towns
detail.abstract: We examine the long-run impact of structural racism on mortgage lending through the lens of “sundown towns,” historical hubs of intense racial exclusion and animus. Using a difference-in-differences design, we isolate the racial animus component from the statistical discrimination and omitted variable bias components of mortgage lending disparities. The racial disparities we find are large, but consistent with statistical discrimination or omitted variables bias, and inconsistent with racial animus. These conclusions are consistent with the idea that oversight and transparency can mitigate taste-based discrimination.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the significance of migration in evaluating the welfare impacts of remote work. By analyzing individual location history data, we first document an increase in net migration towards suburbs and smaller cities in the US since 2020. We demonstrate that the migration wave has been disproportionately fueled by high-income individuals, who were more likely to move due to remote work. Consequently, regions with substantial in-migration observed the greatest rise in housing expenses. This also led to changes in local demand for services and associated employment. Employing a stylized welfare accounting framework, we show that migration mitigated the increase in housing cost burdens for both high- and low-income groups, with the advantages being greater for low-income individuals. Conversely, dispersed job growth, as a result of migration away from major urban centers, curtailed the increase in job accessibility, especially for high-income groups. Factoring in the spatial impacts of migration on housing costs and job accessibility, the welfare inequality surge related to remote work is considerably tempered.

detail.title: Affordable Housing During Childhood Improves Long-term Outcomes of Women and their Children

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Low Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) Program is the largest federal affordable housing program in the U.S. Yet, little is known about its impacts on children and families. This paper shows how LIHTC exposure during childhood affects women’s health outcomes in early-adulthood, as well as the health of their infants. Using geocoded Florida Natality data for 1980-2024 and addresses for LIHTC units we study women born to mothers without any college education between 1980-1999. We use a matching model to compare women born into Census tracts that receive LIHTC during their childhoods to women born into Census tracts without LIHTC during their childhoods. These women and their infants are then observed in adulthood when they first give birth in Florida. We find that a standard deviation increase in childhood LIHTC exposure improves the maternal health index and the infant health index by a small but statistically significant 0.007 standard deviations, and improves an index of maternal SES by 0.005 standard deviations. Given that the average treated tract in our sample has only 0.023 LIHTC units per resident, there is considerable room for increasing exposure. LIHTC exposure during childhood improves outcomes the most for Black women, consistent with Black women being more likely to live in LIHTC units, and also more likely to live in Census tracts that receive LIHTC.

detail.title: Misestimating House Values:  Consequences for Household Finance

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 25-13
publicationDetails.journalName: FRB-Boston: Research Department Working Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: This study examines the effect of systematic household misestimation of home prices on financial decisions, including stockholdings, consumption, and asset allocation. Using exogenous variation in house values, mortgage debt, and homeowner misestimation identified through differences in local housing market characteristics, we find that a $60,000 increase in house overvaluation (approximately one standard deviation) results in a 1.1 to 1.9 percent decrease in risky stockholdings, a 1.5 to 4.3 percent increase in consumption, and a 1.3 to 2.5 percent increase in the share of risk-free assets over liquid wealth. The results highlight the need to better understand how housing wealth and beliefs about house values affect portfolio choice, spending, and overall household finance.
